rows.speaker: أكثم بن صيفي
rows.claim: Aktham ibn Sayfi counts the orphan among four socially abased people, alongside the talebearer, liar, and debtor.
rows.anchor: وقال أكثم بن صيفي: الأذلاء أربعة: النمام، والكذاب، والمديون، واليتيم.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The seeker must not be scolded; this forbids harsh speech, and he should instead receive a small gift or kind answer while being reminded of one's own former poverty.
rows.anchor: أي لا تزجره فهو نهي عن إغلاظ القول. ولكن رده ببذل يسير، أو رد جميل

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada and others say the petitioner should be met with a small gift or gracious reply, and the Prophet should recall his own poverty.
rows.anchor: واذكر فقرك قاله قتادة وغيره

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: Abu Hurayra reports the Prophet forbidding refusal of a petitioner and urging a gift even if the petitioner appears to possess two gold hearts.
rows.anchor: وروي عن أبي هريرة: أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قال:

rows.speaker: إبراهيم بن أدهم
rows.claim: Ibrahim ibn Adham praises petitioners as people who carry the donors' provisions to the afterlife.
rows.anchor: وقال إبراهيم بن أدهم: نعم القوم السؤال: يحملون زادنا إلى الآخرة.

rows.speaker: إبراهيم النخعي
rows.claim: Ibrahim al-Nakha'i says the seeker seeks the afterlife, coming to a household to ask whether they will send anything to their family.
rows.anchor: وقال إبراهيم النخعي: السائل يريد الآخرة، يجيء إلى باب أحدكم فيقول:

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A Prophetic report says to answer petitioners with a small gift or kind word because a nonhuman observer tests how people use God's gifts.
rows.anchor: ردوا السائل ببذل يسير، أو رد جميل، فإنه يأتيكم من ليس من الإنس ولا من الجن

rows.speaker: سفيان
rows.claim: Sufyan interprets the seeker as someone asking about religion, who must be answered gently rather than with harshness or estrangement.
rows.anchor: قاله سفيان. قال ابن العربي: وأما السائل عن الدين فجوابه فرض على العالم،

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Arabi says answering a religious question is a collective obligation for a scholar, like giving alms to a petitioner.
rows.anchor: قال ابن العربي: وأما السائل عن الدين فجوابه فرض على العالم، على الكفاية

rows.speaker: أبو الدرداء
rows.claim: Abu al-Darda welcomed hadith students by spreading his cloak and greeting them as beloved companions of the Messenger.
rows.anchor: وقد كان أبو الدرداء ينظر إلى أصحاب الحديث، ويبسط رداءه لهم،

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Abu Sa'id reports the Prophet saying that students will come from distant regions to learn religion and should be treated well; another wording says they come from the East.
rows.anchor: إن الناس لكم تبع وإن رجالا يأتونكم من أقطار الأرض يتفقهون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The words orphan and seeker are accusatives governed by the verbs after the conditional particle; the implied sense is, whatever happens, do not oppress the orphan or rebuke the seeker.
rows.anchor: و«اليتيم» و«السائل» منصوبان بالفعل الذي بعده وحق المنصوب أن يكون بعد الفاء،

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A Prophetic report recounts God answering the Prophet's comparison with Abraham, Moses, and David by recalling that He sheltered him as an orphan, guided and enriched him, opened his breast, and gave him the closing verses of al-Baqara.
rows.anchor: ألم أجدك يتيما فآويتك؟ ألم أجدك ضالا فهديتك؟ ألم أجدك عائلا فأغنيتك؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command means to publicize God's blessings through gratitude and praise; speaking of blessings and acknowledging them is itself gratitude.
rows.anchor: أي انشر ما أنعم الله عليك بالشكر والثناء. والتحدث بنعم الله، والاعتراف بها شكر.

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid interprets the blessing as the Qur'an, and also as prophethood, meaning the Prophet should convey his commission.
rows.anchor: وروى ابن أبي نجيح عن مجاهد «وأما بنعمة ربك» قال بالقرآن.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although addressed to the Prophet, the ruling applies to him and to everyone else.
rows.anchor: والخطاب للنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم، والحكم عام له ولغيره.

rows.speaker: الحسن بن علي
rows.claim: Hasan ibn Ali advises telling a trusted brother when one receives or does something good.
rows.anchor: وعن الحسن بن علي رضي الله عنهما قال: إذا أصبت خيرا، أو عملت خيرا،

rows.speaker: عمرو بن ميمون
rows.claim: Amr ibn Maymun says a person may tell a trusted brother how much prayer God granted him the previous night.
rows.anchor: وعن عمرو بن ميمون قال: إذا لقي الرجل من إخوانه من يثق به،

rows.speaker: أبو فراس عبد الله بن غالب
rows.claim: Abu Firas regularly recounted his night's recitation, prayer, remembrance, and other good works, defending this by the command to report God's blessing.
rows.anchor: وكان أبو فراس عبد الله بن غالب إذا أصبح يقول: لقد رزقني الله البارحة

rows.speaker: أيوب السختياني وأبو رجاء العطاردي
rows.claim: The same position is also reported from Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani and Abu Raja al-Ataridi.
rows.anchor: ونحوه عن أيوب السختياني وأبي رجاء العطاردي

rows.speaker: بكر بن عبد الله المزني
rows.claim: Bakr ibn Abd Allah al-Muzani attributes to the Prophet the warning that one who receives good but shows no sign of it is hateful to God and hostile to His blessings.
rows.anchor: وقال بكر بن عبد الله المزني قال النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم:

rows.speaker: النعمان بن بشير
rows.claim: Al-Sha'bi transmits from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir a Prophetic saying that gratitude for little entails gratitude for much, gratitude to people is gratitude to God, and voicing blessings is gratitude while suppressing them is ingratitude.
rows.anchor: وروى الشعبي عن النعمان بن بشير قال: قال النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم:

rows.speaker: مالك بن نضلة الجشمي
rows.claim: The Nasa'i report says that when God grants wealth, its effect should be visible on the recipient.
rows.anchor: عن مالك بن نضلة الجشمي قال: كنت عند رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم جالسا، فرآني رث الثياب

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري
rows.claim: Abu Sa'id al-Khudri reports the Prophet saying that God loves beauty and loves to see the effect of His blessing on His servant.
rows.anchor: وروى أبو سعيد الخدري: عن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه قال:

rows.speaker: البزي عن ابن كثير
rows.claim: In al-Bazzi's transmission from Ibn Kathir, the reciter says takbir at the end of Surat al-Duha and between each following sura until completing the Qur'an; Mujahid also transmitted this from Ibn Abbas and Ubayy.
rows.anchor: يكبر القارىء في رواية البزي عن ابن كثير وقد رواه مجاهد عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: أبي بن كعب
rows.claim: A report traced through Ubayy says the Prophet said takbir after al-Duha and between every sura through the end of the Qur'an, pausing between the sura and takbir; it links the practice to the delay in revelation and the Meccan claim that his companion had abandoned him.
rows.anchor: عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم إذا بلغ آخر «والضحى» كبر بين كل سورة تكبيرة،

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says he recited to Ibn Abbas, who instructed him to use the takbir and related it from Ubayy and the Prophet.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد: قرأت على ابن عباس، فأمرني به، وأخبرني به عن أبي عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The other reciters omit takbir because they regard it as a route to adding material to the Qur'an; al-Qurtubi answers that the Qur'an is transmitted by mass transmission and takbir is not Qur'an.
rows.anchor: ولا يكبر في قراءة الباقين لأنها ذريعة إلى الزيادة في القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Takbir is not part of the Qur'an because the Qur'an's suras, verses, and letters are mass-transmitted and takbir is not written in the mushaf, just as the written basmala is not itself Qur'an.
rows.anchor: القرآن ثبت نقلا متواترا سوره وآياته وحروفه لا زيادة فيه ولا نقصان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Takbir is established by solitary transmission as a Sunnah recommended by Ibn Kathir, not an obligation, so leaving it is not an error; al-Hakim graded the report sound though Bukhari and Muslim did not include it.
rows.anchor: أما أنه ثبت سنة بنقل الآحاد، فاستحبه ابن كثير، لا أنه أوجبه فخطأ من تركه.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Opening the breast means opening it to Islam.
rows.anchor: شرح الصدر: فتحه أي ألم نفتح صدرك للإسلام.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, through Abu Salih, interprets the opening as God making the Prophet's heart gentle.
rows.anchor: وروى أبو صالح عن ابن عباس قال: ألم نلين لك قلبك.

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report from Ibn Abbas through al-Dahhak says the Prophet described an opened breast as expansive, marked by detachment from worldly delusion, turning toward the eternal home, and preparing for death before it arrives.
rows.anchor: قالوا يا رسول الله، أينشرح الصدر؟ قال: «نعم وينفسح».

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The same meaning is discussed at the verse about God opening a person's breast to Islam and placing him on light.
rows.anchor: وقد مضى هذا المعنى في «الزمر» عند قوله تعالى:

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan says the Prophet's breast was filled with wisdom and knowledge.
rows.anchor: وروي عن الحسن قال: { ألم نشرح لك صدرك } قال: ملىء حكما وعلما.

rows.speaker: أنس بن مالك
rows.claim: In the sound report from Anas, the Prophet's chest was opened during the night journey, his heart washed with Zamzam water, returned, and filled with faith and wisdom.
rows.anchor: وفي الصحيح عن أنس بن مالك: عن مالك بن صعصعة رجل من قومه أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال:

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Another report says two angels in bird form brought water and snow; one opened the Prophet's breast and the other washed it with its beak.
rows.anchor: وروي عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال:

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A further report describes an angel opening his heart and removing impurity, then praising his retentive heart, seeing eyes, hearing ears, truthful tongue, tranquil self, and fine character.
rows.anchor: وفي حديث آخر قال:

rows.speaker: أهل اللغة
rows.claim: Linguists explain waqi as something that retains what is placed inside it and quthum as comprehensive, as in a person who gathers goodness.
rows.anchor: قال أهل اللغة: قوله: «وكيع أي يحفظ ما يوضع فيه.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the wording asks whether God opened the breast, it means He has opened it: the following past-tense clause about removing the burden coordinates by sense, since surface coordination would have used a present verb.
rows.anchor: فدل هذا على أن معنى «ألم نشرح»: قد شرحنا.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The negative particle lam in a question can turn the negation into confirmation, a grammatical point continued with examples in the following segment.
rows.anchor: و«لم» جحد، وفي الاستفهام طرف من الجحد، وإذا وقع جحد، رجع إلى التحقيق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rhetorical question in al-Tin 95:8 affirms that God is the wisest of judges, and the similar question in al-Zumar 39:36 affirms that God suffices His servant.
rows.anchor: أليس الله بأحكم الحاكمين

rows.speaker: جرير
rows.claim: Jarir's rhetorical question praising Abd al-Malik means that the addressee is indeed best of those who ride camels and most generous.
rows.anchor: ومثله قول جرير يمدح عبد الملك بن مروان:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Removing the burden means taking away the Prophet's sin; Anas's reading is wa-hallalna wa-hatatna, while Ibn Masud reads wa-hallalna anka wiqrak.
rows.anchor: أي حططنا عنك ذنبك. وقرأ أنس «وحللنا، وحططنا».

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This verse parallels the promise to forgive the Prophet's earlier and later sins; some say all the sins concerned preceded prophethood.
rows.anchor: هذه الآية مثل قوله تعالى:

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada, Hasan, and al-Dahhak say the Prophet had sins weighing on him that God forgave.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة والحسن والضحاك: كانت للنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم ذنوب أثقلته فغفرها الله له.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The burden refers to what weighed down the Prophet from his people's pre-Islamic ways, although he never worshipped an idol or image.
rows.anchor: ما كنت فيه من أمر الجاهلية لأنه كان صلى الله عليه وسلم في كثير من مذاهب قومه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The burden made the Prophet's back so heavy that its creaking could be heard; linguists use the same expression for a load that makes a camel's back creak.
rows.anchor: أي أثقله حتى سمع نقيضه أي صوته. وأهل اللغة يقولون:

rows.speaker: جميل
rows.claim: Jamil's line about ropes creaking until their supports nearly break provides poetic evidence for naqidh as a creaking sound under strain.
rows.anchor: قال جميل:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bawani al-zawr means the foundations of the chest, and burden means a heavy load; al-Muhasibi says it would have remained weighty had God not pardoned it.
rows.anchor: «بواني زوره»: أي أصول صدره. فالوزر: الحمل الثقيل. قال المحاسبي:

rows.speaker: المحاسبي
rows.claim: Al-Muhasibi explains why forgiven prophetic sins are described as heavy: prophets are deeply concerned, regretful, and sorrowful about them.
rows.anchor: قال: وإنما وصفت ذنوب الأنبياء بهذا الثقل، مع كونها مغفورة، لشدة اهتمامهم بها،

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi interprets removing the burden as lifting the Prophet's weight; the reading attributed to Abd Allah ibn Masud says the same with wiqrak.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي: «ووضعنا عنك وزرك» أي وحططنا عنك ثقلك.

rows.speaker: الحسين بن الفضل
rows.claim: Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl says the burden refers to slips and inadvertent errors.
rows.anchor: قال الحسين بن الفضل: يعني الخطأ والسهو.

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view takes the burden as the sins of the Prophet's community, attributed to him because his heart was occupied with their plight.
rows.anchor: وقيل: ذنوب أمتك، أضافها إليه لاشتغال قلبه بها.

rows.speaker: عبد العزيز بن يحيى وأبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abd al-Aziz ibn Yahya and Abu Ubayda interpret the burden as the duties of prophethood, which God made lighter.
rows.anchor: وقال عبد العزيز بن يحيى وأبو عبيدة: خففنا عنك أعباء النبوة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another report says revelation initially weighed so heavily that the Prophet nearly cast himself from a mountain until Gabriel appeared and relieved his fear of losing his reason.
rows.anchor: وقيل كان في الابتداء يثقل عليه الوحي، حتى كاد يرمي نفسه من شاهق الجبل،

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A further interpretation is that God protected the Prophet from bearing sin and kept him pure from impurity throughout the forty years before revelation.
rows.anchor: وقيل: عصمناك عن احتمال الوزر، وحفظناك قبل النبوة في الأربعين من الأدناس

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid interprets the raising of the Prophet's mention as its inclusion in the call to prayer.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد: يعني بالتأذين.

rows.speaker: حسان بن ثابت
rows.claim: Hassan ibn Thabit's poem says God joined the Prophet's name with His own in the testimony proclaimed by the caller to prayer.
rows.anchor: وفيه يقول حسان بن ثابت:

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak transmits Ibn Abbas's view that the Prophet is mentioned with God in the adhan, iqama, tashahhud, sermons, festivals, pilgrimage rites, and marriage sermon; denying his messengerhood nullifies a person's worship and makes him an unbeliever.
rows.anchor: وروي عن الضحاك عن ابن عباس، قال: يقول له لا ذكرت إلا ذكرت معي

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view says God raised the Prophet's name in earlier revealed books, commanded previous prophets to announce him, and made his religion prevail over every religion.
rows.anchor: وقيل: أي أعلينا ذكرك، فذكرناك في الكتب المنزلة على الأنبياء قبلك،

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A further view says the Prophet is honored among angels in heaven and believers on earth, and will be raised in the afterlife through the Praised Station and noble ranks.
rows.anchor: وقيل: رفعنا ذكرك عند الملائكة في السماء، وفي الأرض عند المؤمنين،

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وقتادة
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and Qatada say that after prayer the Prophet should strive in supplication and ask God for his need.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس وقتادة: فإذا فرغت من صلاتك { فانصب } أي بالغ في الدعاء

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud interprets the command as turning to night prayer after finishing the obligatory prayers.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن مسعود: إذا فرغت من الفرائض فانصب في قيام الليل.

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi says that after conveying the message the Prophet should seek forgiveness for his sin and for believing men and women.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي: إذا فرغت من تبليغ الرسالة «فانصب» أي استغفر لذنبك

rows.speaker: الحسن وقتادة
rows.claim: Hasan and Qatada also say that after finishing jihad against the enemy one should devote oneself to worship of the Lord.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن وقتادة أيضا: إذا فرغت من جهاد عدوك، فانصب لعبادة ربك.

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid interprets the worldly task as something to finish before engaging in prayer; Hasan has a similar view.
rows.anchor: «فإذا فرغت» من دنياك، «فانصب» في صلاتك.

rows.speaker: الجنيد
rows.claim: Junayd says that when one is done with created beings, one should strive in worship of the Creator.
rows.anchor: وقال الجنيد: إذا فرغت من أمر الخلق، فاجتهد في عبادة الحق.

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Arabi rejects a deviant reading that changes the command into appointing a successor imam, calling both its recitation and interpretation false because the Prophet appointed no successor.
rows.anchor: قال ابن العربي: «ومن المبتدعة من قرأ هذه الآية «فانصب» بكسر الصاد، والهمز من أوله،

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Arabi rejects another ignorant reading with a doubled b as contradicting consensus, though its proposed sense of returning home after jihad is correct and supported by a Prophetic travel report.
rows.anchor: وقرأها بعض: الجهال «فانصب» بتشديد الباء، معناه: إذا فرغت من الجهاد،

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet says travel is a portion of torment that disrupts sleep, food, and drink, so after one's need is met one should hurry back to one's family.
rows.anchor: السفر قطعة من العذاب، يمنع أحدكم نومه وطعامه وشرابه، فإذا قضى أحدكم نهمته،

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Arabi warns that attaching a true meaning to an invented reading or report makes one a liar against God and His Messenger.
rows.anchor: من أخذ معنى صحيحا، فركب عليه من قبل نفسه قراءة أو حديثا، فيكون كاذبا على الله

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر المنصور
rows.claim: Al-Mahdawi reports Abu Ja'far al-Mansur's remote reading of alam nashrah with an open h; it can be explained by a series of changes involving a light nun and a pause form.
rows.anchor: قال المهدوي: وروي عن أبي جعفر المنصور: أنه قرأ:

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: A poetic line about striking the horse's poll exemplifies the proposed imperative with an implicit nūn of emphasis.
rows.anchor: وأنشد عليه: إضرب عنك الهموم طارقها

rows.speaker: أبو السمال
rows.claim: Abu al-Samal reads faraghta with a kasra on the ghayn, a dialect form.
rows.anchor: وروي عن أبي السمال «فإذا فرغت» بكسر الراء، وهي لغة فيه.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reading is farghab, meaning to encourage people toward what God has.
rows.anchor: وقرىء «فرغب» أي فرغب الناس إلى ما عنده.

rows.speaker: شريح
rows.claim: Ibn al-Arabi reports that Shurayh objected to people playing on a festival day, saying the Lawgiver had not commanded it, but Ibn al-Arabi questions this objection.
rows.anchor: روي عن شريح أنه مر بقوم يلعبون يوم عيد، فقال ما بهذا أمر الشارع.

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Arabi counters Shurayh by noting that Abyssinians played with shields and spears in the mosque on Eid while the Prophet watched.
rows.anchor: فإن الحبش كانوا يلعبون بالدرق والحراب في المسجد يوم العيد

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: When Abu Bakr objected to two Ansari girls singing, the Prophet told him to leave them because it was a festival day.
rows.anchor: فقال: «دعهما يا أبا بكر، فإنه يوم عيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Constant, uninterrupted work is not required; sustained application is disliked for ordinary people.
rows.anchor: وليس يلزم الدؤوب على العمل، بل هو مكروه للخلق.

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says tur means mountain and sinin means blessed in Syriac.
rows.anchor: روى ابن أبي نجيح عن مجاهد «وطور» قال: جبل. «سينين» قال: مبارك بالسريانية.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, through Ikrima, says tur is a mountain and sinin means beautiful.
rows.anchor: وعن عكرمة عن ابن عباس قال: «طور» جبل، و«سينين» حسن.

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada likewise interprets sinin as blessed and beautiful.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: سينين هو المبارك الحسن.

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Ikrima identifies it as the mountain from which God spoke to Moses.
rows.anchor: وعن عكرمة قال: الجبل الذي نادى الله جل ثناؤه منه موسى

rows.speaker: مقاتل والكلبي
rows.claim: Muqatil and al-Kalbi say any mountain with fruit-bearing trees is called sinin or sina in Nabataean.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل والكلبي: «سينين» كل جبل فيه شجر مثمر، فهو سينين

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: Amr ibn Maymun reports that Umar recited sina and the secure city in Mecca, raising his voice to honor the sanctuary; in the next rak'a he paired al-Fil with Quraysh.
rows.anchor: وعن عمرو بن ميمون قال: صليت مع عمر بن الخطاب العشاء بمكة،

rows.speaker: النحاس
rows.claim: Al-Nahhas notes that Abd Allah's reading has sina with a kasra under the s, while the report from Umar has it with a fatha.
rows.anchor: النحاس: وفي قراءة عبد الله «سيناء» بكسر السين، وفي حديث عمرو بن ميمون عن عمر بفتح السين.

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash says tur means mountain and sinin means tree, with sininiyya as its singular.
rows.anchor: وقال الأخفش: «طور» جبل. و«سينين» شجر، واحدته «سينينية»

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abu Ali analyzes sinin as fa'lil with a repeated final n, like other forms naming slippery ground, a date-piece, and a tall man.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو علي: «سينين» فعليل، فكررت اللام التي هي نون فيه،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sinin is indeclinable because it is a place or region name, but would take nunation if made a masculine location or house name; the oath invokes a mountain in blessed Syria and the Holy Land.
rows.anchor: وإنما أقسم بهذا الجبل لأنه بالشام والأرض المقدسة، وقد بارك الله فيهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The secure city is Mecca; amin means safe, supported by the description of the sanctuary as secure.
rows.anchor: يعني مكة. سماه أمينا لأنه آمن كما قال:

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra and others take amin to mean safe; a line of poetry uses amini in the same sense.
rows.anchor: فالأمين: بمعنى الآمن قاله الفراء وغيره. قال الشاعر:

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: The argument supports interpreting the fig as Damascus and the olive as Jerusalem: God swears by Damascus, refuge of Jesus; Jerusalem, station of prophets; and Mecca, associated with Abraham and Muhammad.
rows.anchor: احتج من قال: إنه أراد بالتين دمشق، وبالزيتون بيت المقدس.

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One reading addresses the disbeliever in rebuke: since God created humans in the best form, returns them to decrepit age, and moves them through states, what makes them deny resurrection and recompense announced by Muhammad?
rows.anchor: قيل: الخطاب للكافر توبيخا وإلزاما للحجة.

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Another reading addresses the Prophet, telling him to be certain from God's revelation that He is the wisest judge; this is reported from Qatada.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الخطاب للنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أي استيقن مع ما جاءك من الله عز وجل،

rows.speaker: قتادة والفراء
rows.claim: Qatada and al-Farra understand the question to mean who can deny the Messenger after this demonstration of God's power to create humanity, reward, and punish.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة أيضا والفراء: المعنى فمن يكذبك أيها الرسول بعد هذا البيان بالدين.

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Tabari prefers the reading that asks who can deny the Messenger after clear proof of resurrection and recompense.
rows.anchor: واختاره الطبري. كأنه قال: فمن يقدر على ذلك أي على تكذيبك بالثواب والعقاب،

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: The cited line uses the verb dāna to illustrate the sense of what comes afterward or is repeated in later generations.
rows.anchor: قال الشاعر: دنا تميما كما كانت أوائلنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is the most exact and perfect in making all that He creates.
rows.anchor: أي أتقن الحاكمين صنعا في كل ما خلق

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another interpretation says God judges with truth and deals justly among creation.
rows.anchor: وقيل: { بأحكم الحاكمين } قضاء بالحق، وعدلا بين الخلق.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rhetorical question confirms the point against disbelievers who already acknowledge an eternal Creator; a question with a negative can become an affirmative assertion.
rows.anchor: وفيه تقدير لمن اعترف من الكفار بصانع قديم

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Some say the challenge about judgment is abrogated by the sword verse; another view says it remains because there is no conflict, which the author favors.
rows.anchor: وقيل: { فما يكذبك بعد بالدين * أليس الله بأحكم الحاكمين }: منسوخة بآية السيف.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وعلي بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and Ali would answer the verse by saying yes indeed, and that they are witnesses to it; the author selects this practice.
rows.anchor: وكان ابن عباس وعلي بن أبي طالب رضي الله عنهما إذا قرأا { أليس الله بأحكم الحاكمين } قالا: بلى،

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: Al-Tirmidhi transmits from Abu Hurayra that a reciter should answer the verse with yes, and I am among those who witness this.
rows.anchor: ورواه الترمذي عن أبي هريرة قال: من قرأ سورة «والتين والزيتون» فقرأ { أليس الله بأحكم الحاكمين }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most commentators hold that this sura was the first revelation: Gabriel brought its first five verses to Muhammad at Hira; alternatives name al-Muddaththir, al-Fatiha, or al-An'am 6:151, but the first view is correct.
rows.anchor: هذه السورة أول ما نزل من القرآن في قول معظم المفسرين

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: Aisha reports that true dreams began the revelation, followed by the angel's first recitation of the opening verses; Bukhari records it.
rows.anchor: قالت عائشة: أول ما بدىء به رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم الرؤيا الصادقة فجاءه الملك

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: The sound report in both collections describes the Prophet's retreat to Hira, the angel's three embraces when he answered that he could not read, and the revelation of the first five verses.
rows.anchor: أول ما بدىء به رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم من الوحي الرؤيا الصادقة في النوم

rows.speaker: أبو رجاء العطاردي
rows.claim: Abu Raja says Abu Musa taught them this sura in Basra's mosque and identifies it as the first sura revealed to Muhammad.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو رجاء العطاردي: وكان أبو موسى الأشعري يطوف علينا في هذا المسجد: مسجد البصرة،

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: The sequence attributed to Aisha is al-Alaq, al-Qalam, al-Muddaththir, then al-Duha, as cited by al-Mawardi.
rows.anchor: ثم بعدها «والضحى» ذكره الماوردي.

rows.speaker: الزهري
rows.claim: Al-Zuhri transmits that revelation first ran through the words what he did not know; frightened, the Prophet climbed mountain heights until Gabriel reassured him that he was a prophet, after which he returned to Khadija and asked to be covered and given cold water.
rows.anchor: أول ما نزل سورة: { اقرأ باسم ربك } إلى قوله { ما لم يعلم }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Read in the name of the Lord means beginning recitation of the revelation with God's name, including the basmala at the start of each sura; grammatically the prepositional phrase is circumstantial accusative.
rows.anchor: ومعنى { اقرأ باسم ربك } أي اقرأ ما أنزل إليك من القرآن مفتتحا باسم ربك،

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another analysis takes the bā' as meaning on, with the object omitted: read the Qur'an and begin it in God's name.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الباء بمعنى على، أي اقرأ على اسم ربك.

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Some say the name of the Lord is the Qur'an itself and the bā' is extra, as in the phrase about a tree growing with oil and the cited poem about reading suras.
rows.anchor: وقال قوم: اسم ربك هو القرآن، فهو يقول: { اقرأ باسم ربك } أي اسم ربك،

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A further interpretation is simply to invoke God's name and begin recitation with it.
rows.anchor: وقيل: معنى «اقرأ باسم ربك» أي اذكر اسمه. أمره أن يبتدىء القراءة باسم الله.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The human is Adam's descendant; alaq is a clot or congealed blood, distinct from blood that flows, and the plural reflects humanity as a collective created from clots after sperm.
rows.anchor: قوله تعالى: { خلق الإنسان } يعني ابن آدم. { من علق } أي من دم جمع علقة،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A clot is a moist piece of blood named for sticking to things it passes; when dried, it is no longer called a clot.
rows.anchor: والعلقة: قطعة من دم رطب، سميت بذلك لأنها تعلق لرطوبتها بما تمر عليه،

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: The poet's line about blood of the aorta dripping onto hands illustrates the word alaq.
rows.anchor: قال الشاعر: تركناه يخر على يديه يمج عليهما علق الوتين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Humanity is singled out to honor it, and to show the blessing of making a rational, fully formed human from a lowly clot.
rows.anchor: وخص الإنسان بالذكر تشريفا له. وقيل: أراد أن يبين قدر نعمته عليه،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second command to read is emphasis; the sentence then restarts with Lord most generous, meaning generous, as the preceding blessings demonstrate His generosity.
rows.anchor: قوله تعالى: { اقرأ } تأكيد، وتم الكلام، ثم استأنف فقال: { وربك الأكرم } أي الكريم.

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi understands the Most Generous as forbearing toward servants' ignorance and not hastening their punishment.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي: يعني الحليم عن جهل العباد، فلم يعجل بعقوبتهم.

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another interpretation addresses Muhammad: read, and your Lord will help and teach you even though you are not a reader.
rows.anchor: وقيل: «إقرأ وربك» أي اقرأ يا محمد وربك يعينك ويفهمك، وإن كنت غير القارىء.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word al-akram can also mean one who overlooks the ignorance of servants.
rows.anchor: و«الأكرم» بمعنى المتجاوز عن جهل العباد.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Teaching by the pen means teaching writing; Qatada calls the pen a great divine favor, for religion, livelihood, recorded sciences, wisdom, past reports, and revealed books depend on writing.
rows.anchor: يعني الخط والكتابة أي علم الإنسان الخط بالقلم

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says the pen is a tremendous blessing from God, without which religion would not stand and life would not be sound.
rows.anchor: وروى سعيد عن قتادة قال: القلم نعمة من الله تعالى عظيمة، لولا ذلك لم يقم دين،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse highlights the value of writing, through which sciences, judgments, inherited reports, and revealed books are recorded, and explains qalam from cutting, as in clipping a nail.
rows.anchor: وسمي قلما لأنه يقلم أي يقطع، ومنه تقليم الظفر.

rows.speaker: الشعراء المحدثون
rows.claim: A modern poet compares an ink-stained pen tip to an old man courting a young woman and says the pen deserves reverence because pages written with it rise to God.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض الشعراء المحدثين يصف القلم:

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عمر
rows.claim: Ibn Umar asked the Prophet whether he could write down what he heard; the Prophet said yes and cited God's teaching by the pen.
rows.anchor: وعن عبد الله بن عمر قال: يا رسول الله، أأكتب ما أسمع منك من الحديث؟

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid transmits from Ibn Umar that God made four things by His hand before saying Be to other creatures: the pen, Throne, Eden, and Adam.
rows.anchor: وروى مجاهد عن ابن عمر قال: خلق الله عز وجل أربعة أشياء بيده، ثم قال لسائر الحيوان:

rows.speaker: كعب الأحبار
rows.claim: One interpretation says the one taught to write by the pen is Adam, whom Ka'b al-Ahbar calls the first writer.
rows.anchor: أحدها: أنه آدم عليه السلام لأنه أول من كتب، قاله كعب الأحبار.

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: A second view identifies Idris as the first writer, as reported by al-Dahhak.
rows.anchor: الثاني: أنه إدريس، وهو أول من كتب. قاله الضحاك.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The third view is general: God taught all who write, gathering the blessings of human creation and instruction into one account.
rows.anchor: الثالث: أنه أدخل كل من كتب بالقلم لأنه ما علم إلا بتعليم الله سبحانه،

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: A sound report from Abu Hurayra says God wrote in a book above the Throne that His mercy overcomes His wrath.
rows.anchor: الثانية: صح عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم من حديث أبي هريرة، قال:

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A further Prophetic report says the first thing created was the pen, which was commanded to write all events through the Day of Resurrection in the record above the Throne.
rows.anchor: وثبت عنه عليه السلام أنه قال:

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud reports that after forty-two nights an angel shapes the fetus, forms its senses and body, records sex, lifespan, and provision, then departs with the written decree; the Qur'an calls guardian angels noble scribes.
rows.anchor: إذا مر بالنطفة ثنتان وأربعون ليلة، بعث الله إليها ملكا فصورها،

rows.speaker: علماؤنا
rows.claim: The scholars classify three kinds of pens: God's first pen for the decrees, angels' pens for destinies and deeds, and people's pens for speech and practical aims.
rows.anchor: قال علماؤنا: فالأقلام في الأصل ثلاثة: القلم الأول: الذي خلقه الله بيده،

rows.speaker: علماؤنا
rows.claim: Writing has many virtues as a form of communication, which is one of the distinguishing capacities of human beings.
rows.anchor: وفي الكتابة فضائل جمة. والكتابة من جملة البيان، والبيان مما اختص به الآدمي.

rows.speaker: علماؤنا
rows.claim: The scholars say Arabs knew writing less than other peoples, and the Prophet was kept from it so his miracle and proof would be stronger; the discussion is treated in al-Ankabut.
rows.anchor: الثالثة: قال علماؤنا: كانت العرب أقل الخلق معرفة بالكتاب، وأقل العرب معرفة به المصطفى صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: A report from Ibn Masud attributes to the Prophet a prohibition on giving women upper rooms or teaching them writing.
rows.anchor: عن عبد الله بن مسعود، قال: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم:

rows.speaker: علماؤنا
rows.claim: The scholars explain the warning against upper rooms by saying they let women look out at men without providing seclusion, risking mutual temptation; they quote a report that women's good lies in not seeing men or being seen by them.
rows.anchor: قال علماؤنا: وإنما حذرهم النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم ذلك، لأن في إسكانهن الغرف تطلعا إلى الرجل

rows.speaker: علماؤنا
rows.claim: They explain that teaching women writing could enable correspondence with a desired man; writing lets the absent be seen and communicates the inner self without speech, so the Prophet sought to cut off what they regarded as causes of temptation and protect chastity.
rows.anchor: وكذلك تعليم الكتابة ربما كانت سببا للفتنة، وذلك إذا علمت الكتابة كتبت إلى من تهوى.

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One view identifies the human as Adam, taught the names of all things in al-Baqara; Adam recited them to the angels, displaying his rank, establishing his prophethood and God's proof, after which his descendants inherited and transmitted knowledge.
rows.anchor: قيل: «الإنسان» هنا آدم عليه السلام. علمه أسماء كل شيء حسب ما جاء به القرآن

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view identifies the human as Muhammad, based on the statement that God taught him what he had not known; on this reading teaching is future because this was among the earliest revelations.
rows.anchor: وقيل: «الإنسان» هنا الرسول محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم دليله قوله تعالى:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A general interpretation covers humanity, since God brings people from their mothers knowing nothing.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هو عام لقوله تعالى: والله أخرجكم من بطون أمهاتكم لا تعلمون شيئا

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One report says the passage was revealed about Abu Jahl; another says the entire sura came when he barred the Prophet from prayer, which would make it later than the first revelations.
rows.anchor: قوله تعالى: { كلا إن الإنسان ليطغى } إلى آخر السورة. قيل: إنه نزل في أبي جهل.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first five verses may have come first and the remainder later about Abu Jahl, with God ordering their placement together, just as the last-revealed al-Baqara 2:281 was joined to much earlier verses.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون خمس آيات من أولها أول ما نزلت، ثم نزلت البقية في شأن أبي جهل،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kalla here means indeed, since no preceding statement calls for a literal no; the human is Abu Jahl, and transgression is exceeding the limit in disobedience.
rows.anchor: و«كلا» بمعنى حقا إذ ليس قبله شيء. والإنسان هنا أبو جهل. والطغيان: مجاوزة الحد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, through Abu Salih, recounts that Abu Jahl demanded Meccan mountains of gold so he could become wealthy, transgress, and then abandon his faith; Gabriel offered that God could grant it but punish them like the table community, and the Prophet declined to spare them.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس في رواية أبي صالح عنه، قال:

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another interpretation takes seeing oneself as having wealth to mean having a tribe, supporters, and helpers.
rows.anchor: وقيل: «أن رآه استغنى» بالعشيرة والأنصار والأعوان.

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra explains the omitted causal lām and says ra'a takes a subject and predicate like verbs of supposing, so Arabic need not state the reflexive self; he cites forms such as I saw myself and when do you think yourself to be leaving.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء: لم يقل رأى نفسه، كما قيل قتل نفسه لأن رأى من الأفعال التي تريد اسما وخبرا،

rows.speaker: مجاهد وحميد وقنبل عن ابن كثير
rows.claim: Mujahid, Humayd, and Qunbul from Ibn Kathir read ra'ahu with a shortened hamza; the other readers lengthen it, which is preferred.
rows.anchor: وقرأ مجاهد وحميد وقنبل عن ابن كثير «أن رأه استغنى» بقصر الهمزة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A person of this description returns to God to be repaid; raj'a, marja', and ruju' are verbal nouns for returning, with raj'a on the fa'la pattern.
rows.anchor: أي مرجع من هذا وصفه، فنجازيه. والرجعى والمرجع والرجوع: مصادر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The one who forbids prayer is Abu Jahl and the worshipping servant is Muhammad; Abu Jahl threatened to trample the Prophet's neck if he saw him praying, prompting these verses in astonishment.
rows.anchor: قوله تعالى: { أرأيت الذي ينهى } وهو أبو جهل { عبدا } وهو محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم.

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: Abu Hurayra is the authority for Abu Jahl's threat to step on Muhammad's neck if he saw him praying.
rows.anchor: قاله أبو هريرة. فأنزل الله هذه الآيات تعجبا منه.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording contains an ellipsis, asking whether this forbidding man is safe from punishment.
rows.anchor: وقيل: في الكلام حذف والمعنى: أمن هذا الناهي عن الصلاة من العقوبة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rhetorical question asks Abu Jahl whether he realizes that opposing Muhammad, if he is rightly guided and commands piety and prayer, will bring ruin on the opponent.
rows.anchor: أي أرأيت يا أبا جهل إن كان محمد على هذه الصفة، أليس ناهيه عن التقوى والصلاة هالكا؟!

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Jahl rejected God's book and turned away from faith.
rows.anchor: يعني أبا جهل كذب بكتاب الله عز وجل، وأعرض عن الإيمان.

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra reads the three conditional questions together: the servant is guided and commands piety while the forbidding man denies and turns away, making his behavior astonishing; the question about God's seeing him confirms and rebukes, and each later ar'ayta may stand in place of the first.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء: المعنى { أرأيت الذي ينهى * عبدا إذا صلى } وهو على الهدى،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God sees Abu Jahl and knows his conduct; the question is a confirmation and rebuke, and the statement about God's seeing is the answer.
rows.anchor: ألم يعلم أبو جهل بأن الله يرى أي يراه ويعلم فعله فهو تقرير وتوبيخ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If Abu Jahl does not stop harming Muhammad, God will seize him by the forelock and humiliate him; another view places the seizure on Judgment, when he is folded with his feet and cast into Hell.
rows.anchor: قوله تعالى: { كلا لئن لم ينته } أي أبو جهل عن أذاك يا محمد. { لنسفعا } أي لنأخذن { بالناصية } فلنذلنه.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the threat concerns Abu Jahl, it warns everyone who refuses obedience or prevents others from obeying.
rows.anchor: فالآية وإن كانت في أبي جهل فهي عظة للناس، وتهديد لمن يمتنع أو يمنع غيره

rows.speaker: أهل اللغة
rows.claim: Linguists explain saf' as seizing and pulling something forcefully; a line about a bridled horse illustrates taking it by the forelock.
rows.anchor: وأهل اللغة يقولون: سفعت بالشيء: إذا قبضت عليه وجذبته جذبا شديدا.

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: The cited poet describes someone either bridling a colt or seizing it by the forelock, illustrating the verb saf'a.
rows.anchor: قوم إذا كثر الصياح رأيتهم من بين ملجم مهره أو سافع

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another etymology derives the word from the scorching of fire or sun, which darkens a person's face, supported by a line about scorched hearth-stones.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هو مأخوذ من سفعته النار والشمس: إذا غيرت وجهه إلى حال تسويد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The forelock is the hair at the front of the head but can stand for the whole person; taking someone's forelock is an Arab gesture of humiliation.
rows.anchor: والناصية: شعر مقدم الرأس. وقد يعبر بها عن جملة الإنسان

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad says saf' means a hard pull, dragging Abu Jahl by his forelock toward the Fire; another view takes it as a slap, which is close in meaning and can accompany the dragging.
rows.anchor: وقال المبرد: السفع: الجذب بشدة أي لنجرن بناصيته إلى النار.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling the forelock lying and sinful means its owner lies in speech and sins in action; a khati' is culpable, unlike a nonculpable mukhti'.
rows.anchor: أي ناصية أبي جهل كاذبة في قولها، خاطئة في فعلها. والخاطىء معاقب

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: The attribution of lying and sin to the forelock is like describing faces as gazing toward their Lord, or saying a day fasts and a night stands for the person who fasts and prays.
rows.anchor: ووصف الناصية بالكاذبة الخاطئة، كوصف الوجوه بالنظر في قوله تعالى:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word nadi means Abu Jahl's gathering and clan, whom he is invited to call for support.
rows.anchor: أي أهل مجلسه وعشيرته، فليستنصر بهم.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and others say the zabaniah are harsh, forceful angels; lexical authorities give several singular forms and Qatada says the term means police in Arabic.
rows.anchor: أي الملائكة الغلاظ الشداد عن ابن عباس وغيره واحدهم زبني

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisa'i gives zabni as the singular of zabaniah; al-Akhfash, Abu Ubayda, and other authorities offer zābin, zabniya, and zabani, or treat it as a collective.
rows.anchor: وقال الأخفش: زابن. أبو عبيدة: زبنية. وقيل: زباني.

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says zabaniah means police in Arabic and the word derives from pushing or shoving, as in muzabana in sales.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: هم الشرط في كلام العرب. وهو مأخوذ من الزبن وهو الدفع

rows.speaker: أبو الليث السمرقندي
rows.claim: Abu al-Layth al-Samarqandi reports that the angels are called zabaniah because they use their feet as they use their hands.
rows.anchor: حكاه أبو الليث السمرقندي رحمه الله قال: وروي في الخبر أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report says Abu Jahl threatened to summon his clan to protect him, then fled in fear after imagining a mounted angel threatening him with the zabaniah.
rows.anchor: وروي في الخبر أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم لما قرأ هذه السورة، وبلغ إلى قوله تعالى:

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Reports portray the zabaniah as having heads in heaven and feet on earth, pushing unbelievers into Hell; another view calls them the greatest and strongest angels, and the word can describe powerful people.
rows.anchor: وفي الأخبار أن الزبانية رؤوسهم في السماء وأرجلهم في الأرض

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: A poet describes powerful, generous fighters as zabaniah, supporting the word's association with great force.
rows.anchor: قال الشاعر: مطاعيم في القصوى مطاعين في الوغى

rows.speaker: عكرمة عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ikrima reports Ibn Abbas's story that Abu Jahl threatened to trample the Prophet, who said angels would seize him openly; al-Tirmidhi grades this report hasan, sahih, and gharīb.
rows.anchor: وعن عكرمة عن ابن عباس: { سندعو الزبانية } قال:

rows.speaker: عكرمة عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: A second report says Abu Jahl confronted the Prophet at the Maqam, boasted that his clan was the largest assembly, and Ibn Abbas said the punishment angels would have seized him immediately; al-Tirmidhi calls it hasan, gharīb, sahih.
rows.anchor: وروى عكرمة عن ابن عباس قال: مر أبو جهل على النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم وهو يصلي عند المقام،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nadi is the meeting place where people gather, but here it means the people of the meeting place, as in the poetic citation.
rows.anchor: والنادي في كلام العرب: المجلس الذي ينتدي فيه القوم أي يجتمعون،

rows.speaker: جرير
rows.claim: Jarir's line about a council of gray-whiskered, submissive men gives poetic evidence for nadi as a meeting assembly.
rows.anchor: لهم مجلس صهب السبال أذلة

rows.speaker: زهير
rows.claim: Zuhayr's line about fine-looking stations or assemblies provides another poetic example for the gathering-place sense.
rows.anchor: وقال زهير: وفيهم مقامات حسان وجوههم

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: An unnamed poet uses majlis as the place where people meet and contend after Kulaib's death.
rows.anchor: وقال آخر: واستب بعدك يا كليب المجلس

rows.speaker: زهير
rows.claim: Zuhayr's line about a neighbor and the man invited to the gathering shows nadaytu can mean to sit with someone.
rows.anchor: وقد ناديت الرجل أناديه إذا جالسته. قال زهير: وجار البيت والرجل المنادي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kalla denies Abu Jahl's expectation; Muhammad must not obey him by abandoning prayer, but should pray to God and approach through obedience and worship.
rows.anchor: أي ليس الأمر على ما يظنه أبو جهل. { لا تطعه } أي فيما دعاك إليه من ترك الصلاة.

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another interpretation says that while prostrating, the worshipper should approach God through supplication.
rows.anchor: وقيل: المعنى: إذا سجدت فاقترب من الله بالدعاء.

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: Ata reports Abu Hurayra transmitting the Prophet's saying that the servant is closest and most beloved to God when his forehead is on the ground in prostration.
rows.anchor: روى عطاء عن أبي هريرة قال: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم:

rows.speaker: علماؤنا
rows.claim: The scholars explain prostration as the culmination of servitude and humility before God's unmatched might; greater distance from the human condition brings nearness to Paradise and God's abode.
rows.anchor: قال علماؤنا: وإنما كان ذلك لأنها نهاية العبودية والذلة ولله غاية العزة،

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A sound hadith instructs worshippers to glorify God in bowing and strive in supplication during prostration, when prayers are likely to be answered.
rows.anchor: وفي الحديث الصحيح: أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال:

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: The cited couplet says that when necks humble themselves before God, their dignity lies in that very abasement.
rows.anchor: ولقد أحسن من قال: وإذا تذللت الرقاب تواضعا

rows.speaker: زيد بن أسلم
rows.claim: Zayd ibn Aslam interprets the command as Muhammad prostrating in prayer while Abu Jahl approaches the Fire.
rows.anchor: وقال زيد بن أسلم: اسجد أنت يا محمد مصليا، واقترب أنت يا أبا جهل من النار.

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Prostration could mean prayer prostration or the recitation prostration; Ibn al-Arabi says prayer is the apparent sense from the context, but the sound report from Abu Hurayra in Muslim explicitly establishes a recitation prostration here.
rows.anchor: قال ابن العربي: «والظاهر أنه سجود الصلاة» لقوله تعالى:

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: Abu Hurayra says he prostrated with the Prophet in al-Inshiqaq and in Iqra, establishing that this passage involves prostration of recitation.
rows.anchor: لولا ما ثبت في الصحيح من رواية مسلم وغيره من الأئمة عن أبي هريرة أنه قال:

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: A report from Ali says the four obligatory prostration passages are Alif Lam Mim, Ha Mim Tanzil, al-Najm, and Iqra; Ibn al-Arabi notes that accepting this implies a second prostration in al-Hajj, though it occurs with bowing.
rows.anchor: وقد روى ابن وهب، عن حماد بن زيد، عن عاصم بن بهدلة، عن زر بن حبيش، عن علي بن أبي طالب رضي الله عنه قال:

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Ibn Nafi and Mutarrif say Malik privately prostrated at the end of this sura, while Ibn Wahb considered it one of the obligatory prostrations.
rows.anchor: وقد قال ابن نافع ومطرف: وكان مالك يسجد في خاصة نفسه بخاتمة هذه السورة

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: A report transmitted through Malik, Rabi'a, and Nafi says that when this sura was revealed the Prophet told Muadh to write it; the tablet, pen, and inkwell bowed and prayed for exalted remembrance, removal of burdens, and forgiveness, after which Muadh and the Prophet prostrated.
rows.anchor: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم لمعاذ: «اكتبها يا معاذ» فأخذ معاذ اللوح والقلم والنون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in We sent it refers to the Qur'an, whose identity is understood although unnamed here because the Qur'an is like one sura.
rows.anchor: يعني القرآن وإن لم يجر له ذكر في هذه السورة لأن المعنى معلوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an says it was revealed in Ramadan and on a blessed night, identifying that night with Laylat al-Qadr.
rows.anchor: شهر رمضان الذي أنزل فيه القرآن

rows.speaker: الشعبي
rows.claim: Al-Sha'bi says the revelation of the Qur'an began on Laylat al-Qadr.
rows.anchor: وقال الشعبي: المعنى إنا ابتدأنا إنزاله في ليلة القدر.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Another account says the entire Qur'an descended from the Preserved Tablet to the lowest heaven, at Bayt al-Izza, on Laylat al-Qadr, then Gabriel revealed it piecemeal to the Prophet over twenty-three years.
rows.anchor: وقيل: بل نزل به جبريل عليه السلام جملة واحدة في ليلة القدر، من اللوح المحفوظ

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Mawardi's version says the whole Qur'an reached the scribal angels in the lowest heaven, who gave it to Gabriel over twenty years and Gabriel to the Prophet over twenty; Ibn al-Arabi rejects this because no intermediary stands between God and Gabriel or Gabriel and Muhammad.
rows.anchor: وحكى الماوردي عن ابن عباس قال: نزل القرآن في شهر رمضان، وفي ليلة القدر،

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid interprets qadr as judgment, the night on which God determines deaths, lifespans, provisions, and other matters until the next year and gives them to four angels charged with affairs.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد: في ليلة الحكم. { ومآ أدراك ما ليلة القدر } قال: ليلة الحكم.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says what is in the Preserved Record is written for the coming year, including provision, rain, life, death, and pilgrims; Ikrima and Sa'id ibn Jubayr add that pilgrims are listed by name and none are omitted or added.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس قال: يكتب من أم الكتاب ما يكون في السنة من رزق ومطر وحياة وموت،

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Another report from Ibn Abbas says God determines decrees on mid-Sha'ban and passes them to their agents on Laylat al-Qadr.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس أيضا: أن الله تعالى يقضي الأقضية في ليلة نصف شعبان،

rows.speaker: الزهري
rows.claim: Some explain the name as referring to the night’s greatness, rank, and honor; al-Zuhri cites the ordinary sense of a person's standing.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إنما سميت بذلك لعظمها وقدرها وشرفها من قولهم: لفلان قدر أي شرف ومنزلة.

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Other explanations tie the name to the great worth and reward of worship, the elevation of a previously low-status worshipper, the high rank of the revealed book and its recipients, the angels' status, or the blessings and forgiveness God sends.
rows.anchor: وقيل: سميت بذلك لأن للطاعات فيها قدرا عظيما، وثوابا جزيلا.

rows.speaker: سهل
rows.claim: Sahl says the night is named qadr because God assigns mercy to the believers in it.
rows.anchor: وقال سهل: سميت بذلك لأن الله تعالى قدر فيها الرحمة على المؤمنين.

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalil says the earth is constricted on that night by the angels; the following segment supplies the linguistic evidence from al-Talaq.
rows.anchor: وقال الخليل: لأن الأرض تضيق فيها بالملائكة كقوله تعالى:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about provision being constricted in al-Talaq uses qadara in the sense of narrowing or making constricted.
rows.anchor: ومن قدر عليه رزقه [الطلاق: 7] أي ضيق.

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra says every Quranic phrase ma adraka signals that God has informed the listener, whereas ma yudrika signals that He has not; Sufyan agrees.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: كل ما في القرآن من قوله تعالى: { ومآ أدراك } فقد أدراه.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse emphasizes the night’s virtue: the value of a time depends on the amount of good done in it, and that night's abundant good surpasses what appears in a thousand months.
rows.anchor: بين فضلها وعظمها. وفضيلة الزمان إنما تكون بكثرة ما يقع فيه من الفضائل.

rows.speaker: كثير من المفسرين
rows.claim: Many commentators say worship on Laylat al-Qadr is better than worship during a thousand months that contain no such night.
rows.anchor: وقال كثير من المفسرين: أي العمل فيها خير من العمل في ألف شهر ليس فيها ليلة القدر.

rows.speaker: أبو العالية
rows.claim: Abu al-Aliya specifies that the thousand months have no Laylat al-Qadr in them.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو العالية: ليلة القدر خير من ألف شهر لا تكون فيه ليلة القدر.

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Some take a thousand months as an Arabic hyperbole for all time, like the thousand years in al-Baqara 2:96.
rows.anchor: وقيل: عنى بألف شهر جميع الدهر لأن العرب تذكر الألف في غاية الأشياء

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another explanation says worshippers once needed eighty-three years and four months to earn the title worshipper, so God gave Muhammad's community one night better than that span.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إن العابد كان فيما مضى لا يسمى عابدا حتى يعبد الله ألف شهر،

rows.speaker: أبو بكر الوراق
rows.claim: Abu Bakr al-Warraq says Sulaiman's and Dhul-Qarnayn's kingdoms each lasted five hundred months, so worship that night is better than possessing their combined thousand-month rule.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو بكر الوراق: كان ملك سليمان خمسمائة شهر، وملك ذي القرنين خمسمائة شهر

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud reports that Muslims were amazed by a man of Israel who armed himself for God's cause for a thousand months, and the sura came to say Laylat al-Qadr is better than those months; a similar report is attributed to Ibn Abbas.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن مسعود: إن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم ذكر رجلا من بني إسرائيل لبس السلاح في سبيل الله ألف شهر

rows.speaker: وهب بن منبه
rows.claim: Wahb says the Israelite was named Shamsun: dedicated by his mother, he fought idolaters alone with camel jawbones, received water from them when thirsty, and could not be hurt by iron.
rows.anchor: وهب بن منبه: إن ذلك الرجل كان مسلما، وإن أمه جعلته نذرا لله،

rows.speaker: كعب الأحبار
rows.claim: Ka'b al-Ahbar tells of an Israelite king granted a thousand sons, each equipped to fight for a month before dying; while the king prayed and fasted, he prepared all of them, then fought and died, and the night was declared better than his thousand months of worship and jihad.
rows.anchor: وقال كعب الأحبار: كان رجلا ملكا في بني إسرائيل، فعل خصلة واحدة،

rows.speaker: علي وعروة
rows.claim: Ali and Urwa report that the Prophet named four Israelites who worshipped for eighty years without sin—Job, Zechariah, Ezekiel son of the old woman, and Joshua son of Nun; Gabriel told him his community was granted better, and the Prophet rejoiced.
rows.anchor: ذكر النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أربعة من بني إسرائيل، فقال: «عبدوا الله ثمانين سنة،

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Malik says the Prophet was shown the lifespans of earlier peoples and feared his community could not match their deeds, so God gave him Laylat al-Qadr, better than a thousand months.
rows.anchor: وقال مالك في الموطأ من رواية ابن القاسم وغيره: سمعت من أثق به يقول: إن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم أري أعمار الأمم قبله،

rows.speaker: الحسن بن علي
rows.claim: A Tirmidhi report from Hasan ibn Ali says the Prophet was shown Umayyads on his pulpit and was saddened; al-Kawthar was revealed and interpreted as a river in Paradise, and the Laylat al-Qadr verses as their thousand-month rule after him; al-Qasim counted exactly one thousand months, and the report is called gharīb.
rows.anchor: وفي الترمذي عن الحسن بن علي رضي الله عنهما:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The angels descend from every heaven and from the Lote Tree, where Gabriel resides, reaching earth and saying amen to people's prayers until dawn.
rows.anchor: أي تهبط من كل سماء، ومن سدرة المنتهى ومسكن جبريل على وسطها.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Spirit is Gabriel; al-Qushayri also reports a distinct order of spirits who guard the other angels and remain unseen by them as angels are unseen by humans.
rows.anchor: والروح فيها بإذن ربهم } أي جبريل عليه السلام. وحكى القشيري: أن الروح صنف من الملائكة

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil says the spirits are the noblest angels and nearest to God.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل: هم أشرف الملائكة وأقربهم من الله تعالى.

rows.speaker: مجاهد عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: Another report transmitted by Mujahid from Ibn Abbas as a Prophetic statement identifies them as an army of God other than angels; al-Qushayri also mentions created beings with hands and feet who eat.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إنهم جند من جند الله عز وجل من غير الملائكة. رواه مجاهد عن ابن عباس مرفوعا

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view says the Spirit is an immense creature standing in one rank while the angels stand in another.
rows.anchor: وقيل: «الروح» خلق عظيم يقوم صفا، والملائكة كلهم صفا.

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Some interpret the Spirit as mercy carried by Gabriel and the angels, supported by al-Nahl 16:2 where the Spirit from God's command means mercy.
rows.anchor: وقيل: «الروح» الرحمة ينزل بها جبريل عليه السلام مع الملائكة في هذه الليلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here means on Laylat al-Qadr, by permission means by God's command, and every command means all that God decreed for the year ahead, like the expression in al-Ra'd 13:11.
rows.anchor: فيها } أي في ليلة القدر. { بإذن ربهم } أي بأمره. { من كل أمر }: أمر بكل أمر قدره الله

rows.speaker: البزي
rows.claim: Most readers pronounce tanazzalu with an open t, while al-Bazzi doubles the t; Talha ibn Musarrif and Ibn al-Sumayqa' read it in the passive with a u vowel.
rows.anchor: وقراءة العامة «تنزل» بفتح التاء إلا أن البزي شدد التاء.

rows.speaker: علي وابن عباس وعكرمة والكلبي
rows.claim: Ali, Ibn Abbas, Ikrima, and al-Kalbi read min kulli imri', meaning every person; al-Kalbi says Gabriel and the angels greet every Muslim, with min used to mean upon.
rows.anchor: وقرأ علي وابن عباس وعكرمة والكلبي «من كل امرىء».

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: Anas reports that on Laylat al-Qadr Gabriel descends among a great host of angels, praying and greeting every servant who stands or sits remembering God.
rows.anchor: إذا كان ليلة القدر نزل جبريل في كبكبة من الملائكة،

rows.speaker: نافع
rows.claim: Some, including Nafi, end the previous sentence at min kulli amr and begin a new sentence with salam.
rows.anchor: قيل: إن تمام الكلام { من كل أمر } ثم قال { سلام }. روي ذلك عن نافع وغيره

rows.speaker: نافع
rows.claim: Nafi and others say the night is entirely safety and good, without evil.
rows.anchor: أي ليلة القدر سلامة وخير كلها لا شر فيها

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak says God decrees only safety on this night, whereas on other nights He decrees both afflictions and safety.
rows.anchor: قال الضحاك: لا يقدر الله في تلك الليلة إلا السلامة، وفي سائر الليالي يقضي بالبلايا

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Another sense is that Satan cannot do evil or harm to believing men and women on the night; Mujahid calls it a safe night, and the report is also transmitted as Prophetic.
rows.anchor: وكذا قال مجاهد: هي ليلة سالمة، لا يستطيع الشيطان أن يعمل فيها سوءا ولا أذى.

rows.speaker: الشعبي
rows.claim: Al-Sha'bi says the angels greet people in mosques from sunset until dawn, passing each believer with a greeting of peace.
rows.anchor: وقال الشعبي: هو تسليم الملائكة على أهل المساجد، من حين تغيب الشمس

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another interpretation takes the greeting as angels greeting one another.
rows.anchor: وقيل: يعني سلام الملائكة بعضهم على بعض فيها.

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada interprets salam as goodness.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: { سلام هي }: خير هي.

rows.speaker: الكسائي وابن محيصن
rows.claim: Al-Kisa'i and Ibn Muhaysin read matli' with a kasra on the l; the other readers use a fatha. Both are verbal-noun dialect forms, with the fatha regular and the kasra an irregular pattern like the cited examples.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الكسائي وابن محيصن «مطلع» بكسر اللام، الباقون بالفتح.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fatha is expected for the form fa'ala yaf'alu, while the kasra is an irregular pattern like mashriq, maghrib, manbit, maskan, mansak, mahshar, masqat, and majzar; both refer to the verbal noun rather than place noun.
rows.anchor: والفتح الأصل في فعل يفعل نحو المقتل والمخرج. والكسر على أنه مما شذ عن قياسه

rows.speaker: أبي بن كعب
rows.claim: Most scholars place Laylat al-Qadr on the twenty-seventh night: Ubayy tells Zirr that Ibn Masud's year-long vigil statement aimed to keep people from relying on one date, though Ubayy knew it was among the last ten and specifically the twenty-seventh; he swears to it and cites the Prophet's sign that its sunrise has no rays. Tirmidhi grades the report hasan sahih and Muslim transmits it.
rows.anchor: والذي عليه المعظم أنها ليلة سبع وعشرين لحديث زر بن حبيش قال: قلت لأبي بن كعب:

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: Some hold that the night occurs in Ramadan rather than throughout the year, a view attributed to Abu Hurayra and others.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هي في شهر رمضان دون سائر العام قاله أبو هريرة وغيره.

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view allows Laylat al-Qadr to occur on any night of the year; a conditional divorce or manumission then takes effect only after a year passes because its date is uncertain and no specific date is established.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هي في ليالي السنة كلها. فمن علق طلاق امرأته أو عتق عبده بليلة القدر،

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: Abu Hanifa holds that the night can occur anywhere in the whole year; Ibn Masud and Ibn Umar say the year-long vigil advice was meant to keep people from becoming complacent.
rows.anchor: وإلى هذا القول ذهب أبو حنيفة أنها في جميع السنة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Some say Laylat al-Qadr was lifted and occurred only once, but the author says the correct view is that it continues to recur.
rows.anchor: وقيل عنه: إنها رفعت يعني ليلة القدر وأنها إنما كانت مرة واحدة والصحيح أنها باقية.

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud says its calendar date changes from one year to the next, while the majority say it recurs every Ramadan.
rows.anchor: وروي عن ابن مسعود أيضا: أنها إذا كانت في يوم من هذه السنة، كانت في العام المقبل في يوم آخر.

rows.speaker: أبو رزين العقيلي
rows.claim: Abu Razin al-Uqayli identifies it as the first night of Ramadan.
rows.anchor: ثم قيل: إنها الليلة الأولى من الشهر قاله أبو رزين العقيلي.

rows.speaker: الحسن وابن إسحاق وعبد الله بن الزبير
rows.claim: Hasan, Ibn Ishaq, and Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr place it on the seventeenth night, the eve of Badr, citing al-Anfal's Day of Criterion; another view says the nineteenth.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن وابن إسحاق وعبد الله بن الزبير: هي ليلة سبع عشرة من رمضان،

rows.speaker: مالك والشافعي والأوزاعي وأبو ثور وأحمد
rows.claim: The well-known and correct view is that it falls during the last ten nights of Ramadan, held by Malik, al-Shafi'i, al-Awza'i, Abu Thawr, and Ahmad.
rows.anchor: والصحيح المشهور: أنها في العشر الأواخر من رمضان وهو قول مالك والشافعي والأوزاعي وأبي ثور وأحمد.

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Some specify the twenty-first night, a view toward which al-Shafi'i inclined based on the water-and-mud report transmitted by Abu Sa'id and Malik.
rows.anchor: ثم قال قوم: هي ليلة الحادي والعشرين. ومال إليه الشافعي رضي الله عنه،

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: A man dreamed that the night was the seventh remaining; the Prophet said their dreams converged on the twenty-third and advised anyone who wished to pray during the month to pray that night. Ma'mar says Ayyub bathed and applied perfume then.
rows.anchor: وقيل ليلة الثالث والعشرين لما رواه ابن عمر:

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن أنيس
rows.claim: In Muslim, the Prophet says he saw himself prostrating on a dawn of mud and water; Abd Allah ibn Anis says he saw the Prophet's predicted sign on the morning of the twenty-third.
rows.anchor: قال عبد الله بن أنيس: فرأيته في صبيحة ليلة ثلاث وعشرين في الماء والطين،

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري
rows.claim: A report from Abu Sa'id has the Prophet instruct people to seek the night on the ninth, seventh, or fifth night remaining in the last ten; Malik maps these to the twenty-first, twenty-third, and twenty-fifth.
rows.anchor: وقيل: ليلة خمس وعشرين لحديث أبي سعيد الخدري: أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قال:

rows.speaker: علي وعائشة ومعاوية وأبي بن كعب
rows.claim: The twenty-seventh-night view, whose evidence was given in the previous segment, is attributed to Ali, Aisha, Muawiya, and Ubayy; the text begins another Ibn Umar report but gives no further content in this chunk.
rows.anchor: وقيل: ليلة سبع وعشرين. وقد مضى دليله، وهو قول علي رضي الله عنه وعائشة ومعاوية وأبي بن كعب.
